body_text: PDF Version MINNEAPOLIS, July 23, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- CVRx, Inc. (NASDAQ: CVRX) ("CVRx"), a commercial-stage medical device company focused on developing, manufacturing and commercializing innovative neuromodulation solutions for patients with cardiovascular diseases, today announced that it plans to release second quarter 2026 financial and operating results after market close on Thursday, August 6, 2026. The Company will host a conference call to review its results at 4:30 p.m. Eastern Time the same day. A live webcast of the investor conference call will be available online at the investor relations page of the Company’s website at ir.cvrx.com . To listen to the conference call on your telephone, please dial 1- 877-704-4453 for U.S. callers, or 1-201-389-0920 for international callers, approximately ten minutes prior to the start time. About CVRx, Inc. CVRx is a commercial-stage medical device company focused on developing, manufacturing and commercializing innovative neuromodulation solutions for patients with cardiovascular diseases. Barostim™ is the first medical technology approved by FDA that uses neuromodulation to improve the symptoms of patients with heart failure. Barostim is an implantable device that delivers electrical pulses to baroreceptors located in the wall of the carotid artery. The therapy is designed to restore balance to the autonomic nervous system and thereby reduce the symptoms of heart failure. Barostim received the FDA Breakthrough Device designation and is FDA-approved for use in heart failure patients in the U.S. It has been certified as compliant with the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR) and holds CE Mark for heart failure and resistant hypertension in the European Economic Area. To learn more about Barostim, visit www.cvrx.com. title: Vertiv expects powering up for AI, digital twins and adaptive liquid cooling to shape data center design and operations
summary: Data center innovation is continuing to be shaped by macro forces and technology trends related to AI, according to a report from Vertiv (NYSE: VRT), a global leader in critical digital infrastructure. The Vertiv™ Frontiers report, which draws on expertise from across the organization, details the technology trends driving current and future innovation, from powering up for AI, to digital twins, to adaptive liquid cooling.
body_text: COLUMBUS, Ohio [January 8, 2026] – Data center innovation is continuing to be shaped by macro forces and technology trends related to AI, according to a report from Vertiv (NYSE: VRT), a global leader in critical digital infrastructure. The Vertiv™ Frontiers report , which draws on expertise from across the organization, details the technology trends driving current and future innovation, from powering up for AI, to digital twins, to adaptive liquid cooling. “The data center industry is continuing to rapidly evolve how it designs, builds, operates and services data centers, in response to the density and speed of deployment demands of AI factories,” said Vertiv chief product and technology officer, Scott Armul. “We see cross-technology forces, including extreme densification, driving transformative trends such as higher voltage DC power architectures and advanced liquid cooling that are important to deliver the gigawatt scaling that is critical for AI innovation. On-site energy generation and digital twin technology are also expected to help to advance the scale and speed of AI adoption.” The Vertiv Frontiers report builds on and expands Vertiv’s previous annual Data Center Trends predictions . The report identifies macro forces driving data center innovation: extreme densification—accelerated by AI and HPC workloads; gigawatt scaling at speed—data centers are now being deployed rapidly and at unprecedented scale; data center as a unit of compute—the AI era requires facilities to be built and operated as a single system; and silicon diversification—data center infrastructure must adapt to an increasing range of chips and compute. The report details how these macro forces have in turn shaped five key trends impacting specific areas of the data center landscape. Powering up for AI Most current data centers still rely on hybrid AC/DC power distribution from the grid to the IT racks, which includes three to four conversion stages and some inefficiencies. This existing approach is under strain as power densities increase, largely driven by AI workloads. The shift to higher voltage DC architectures enables significant reductions in current, size of conductors, and number of conversion stages while centralizing power conversion at the room level. Hybrid AC and DC systems are pervasive, but as full DC standards and equipment mature, higher voltage DC is likely to become more prevalent as rack densities increase. On-site generation, and microgrids, will also drive adoption of higher voltage DC. Distributed AI The billions of dollars invested into AI data centers to support large language models (LLMs) to date have been aimed at supporting widespread adoption of AI tools by consumers and businesses. Vertiv believes AI is becoming increasingly critical to businesses but how, and from where, those inference services are delivered will depend on the specific requirements and conditions of the organization. While this will impact businesses of all types, highly regulated industries, such as finance, defense, and healthcare, may need to maintain private or hybrid AI environments via on-premise data centers, due to data residency, security, or latency requirements. Flexible, scalable high-density power and liquid cooling systems could enable capacity through new builds or retrofitting of existing facilities. Energy autonomy accelerates Short-term on-site energy generation capacity has been essential for most standalone data centers for decades, to support resiliency. However, widespread power availability challenges are creating conditions to adopt extended energy autonomy, especially for AI data centers. Investment in on-site power generation, via natural gas turbines and other technologies, does have several intrinsic benefits but is primarily driven by power availability challenges. Technology strategies such as Bring Your Own Power (and Cooling) are likely to be part of ongoing energy autonomy plans. Digital twin-driven design and operations With increasingly dense AI workloads and more powerful GPUs also come a demand to deploy these complex AI factories with speed. Using AI-based tools, data centers can be mapped and specified virtually, via digital twins, and the IT and critical digital infrastructure can be integrated, often as prefabricated modular designs, and deployed as units of compute, reducing time-to-token by up to 50%. This approach will be important to efficiently achieving the gigawatt-scale buildouts required for future AI advancements. Adaptive, resilient liquid cooling AI workloads and infrastructure have accelerated the adoption of liquid cooling. But conversely, AI can also be used to further refine and optimize liquid cooling solutions. Liquid cooling has become mission-critical for a growing number of operators but AI could provide ways to further enhance its capabilities. AI, in conjunction with additional monitoring and control systems, has the potential to make liquid cooling systems smarter and even more robust by predicting potential failures and effectively managing fluid and components. This trend should lead to increasing reliability and uptime for high value hardware and associated data/workloads. Vertiv does business in more than 130 countries, delivering critical digital infrastructure solutions to data centers, communication networks, and commercial and industrial facilities worldwide. The company's comprehensive portfolio spans power management, thermal management, and IT infrastructure solutions and services—from the cloud to the network edge. This integrated approach enables continuous operations, optimal performance, and scalable growth for customers navigating an increasingly complex digital landscape. For more information on Vertiv solutions or Vertiv™ Frontiers data center trends predictions, visit Vertiv.com . About Vertiv Vertiv (NYSE: VRT) brings together hardware, software, analytics and ongoing services to enable its customers’ vital applications to run continuously, perform optimally and grow with their business needs. Vertiv solves the most important challenges facing today’s data centers, communication networks and commercial and industrial facilities with a portfolio of power, cooling and IT infrastructure solutions and services that extends from the cloud to the edge of the network. Headquartered in Westerville, Ohio, USA, Vertiv does business in more than 130 countries. For more information, and for the latest news and content from Vertiv, visit Vertiv.com . title: Best tools for finding small business decision-makers (2026)
summary: Apollo and ZoomInfo miss 60%+ of small business owners. Compare tools built to find the owner behind the bu...
body_text: Quick answer: Openmart is built to find the owner behind a small business, not just employees at larger companies — the opposite search order from Apollo, ZoomInfo, and most B2B databases. In a 1,000-record benchmark, Openmart matched 87–91% of businesses under 10 employees, versus 36–56% for Apollo and ZoomInfo. Free plan available with 50 searches/month, no credit card required. An SDR gets handed a new vertical on a Monday: find decision-makers at HVAC companies in the Southeast. She opens Apollo , filters by industry and company size, exports 60 contacts, and starts dialing. By Wednesday she's learned that 40 of those contacts are front-desk staff or a generic info@ inbox. The actual owner — the person who decides whether to buy — isn't in the export at all. This isn't a fluke. It's what happens when a tool built to find employees gets pointed at businesses that don't have any. Why small business decision-makers don't show up in most databases Enterprise prospecting tools are built around one assumption: the decision-maker has a title, a LinkedIn profile, and a company with an org chart underneath them. That assumption holds for a 500-person software company. It falls apart for a 12-person HVAC contractor, where the owner runs the crew, answers the phone, and has never once updated a LinkedIn profile. Openmart is built to find the owner behind the business , not to hunt for employees at larger companies. That's a different search problem than the one Apollo, ZoomInfo, and most B2B databases were designed to solve, and it shows up directly in the data: in a 1,000-record benchmark , Apollo and ZoomInfo failed to return any contact for 36–56% of businesses under 10 employees. Openmart matched 87–91% of the same segment. What this costs an SDR specifically The SDR problem isn't data quality in the abstract, it's time. Every hour spent manually verifying whether a contact is actually the owner, or clicking through a business's "About" page hunting for a name, is an hour not spent dialing. A rep working a fresh vertical every few weeks can't afford to rebuild a research process from scratch each time. Openmart's owner finder attaches owner name, verified email, and direct phone to each business record before it ever reaches a rep's list — filterable by category, location, and size. There's no cross-referencing a LinkedIn export against a separate company list. The record that comes back is the person who owns the business. What this costs a startup specifically A startup selling into local business or SMB verticals faces the same wall with less room to absorb it. Most early-stage teams have no dedicated sales ops function, and the ICP is often still moving as the product finds its footing. Time spent configuring a custom enrichment workflow for a target segment that might change next quarter is time the team doesn't have. That's the case for starting with a database that returns owner contacts on a simple filter rather than a platform that requires building a pipeline first. Openmart's free plan includes 50 searches a month with no credit card required, which is enough to test data quality against a real target list before committing to anything. Best tools for finding small business decision-makers Openmart — best for verified owner contacts at scale Every record includes the owner's name, verified email, and direct phone, pulled from Google Maps listings and business registries and checked before delivery, not scraped and hoped for. Apollo.io — best for contacts that already have a LinkedIn presence Strong database for mid-market and enterprise contacts. Coverage of owner-operated businesses is thin, since Apollo starts from a person's professional profile and works backward to the company. Clay — best for technical teams building custom enrichment pipelines Flexible for chaining data sources and scoring leads, but the workflow has to be built before it returns anything. Not a same-day solution for a rep who needs a list this afternoon. ZoomInfo — best for enterprise accounts with budget to match Deep data on Fortune 500 org charts. Not built to index small or owner-operated businesses, and priced well outside what a startup or lean SDR team typically has to spend. Comparison: tools for finding small business decision-makers Tool Free Plan Starting Price Owner-Level Accuracy Best For Openmart Yes (200 credits/mo) $105/mo 97–99% SDRs and startups selling to SMBs/local businesses Apollo.io Yes (900 annual credits) $49/mo Low for owner-operated firms Tech-adjacent SMBs with LinkedIn presence Clay Yes (500 actions/mo) $167/mo Depends on workflow built Technical RevOps teams ZoomInfo No ~$15,000/yr Low for owner-operated firms Enterprise AEs How to choose If the business has a LinkedIn presence — SaaS, agencies, professional services — a contact-first tool like Apollo works fine, because the decision-maker actually shows up there. If the business is owner-operated — local services, contractors, independent retail — that search order doesn't work, because the decision-maker was never on LinkedIn to begin with. Openmart's local business database starts from the business and attaches the owner, which is the search order that segment actually needs. If a startup's ICP is still shifting, avoid a tool that requires setup before it returns a result. Query by category and location, see the data quality against a real list, and decide from there. Frequently asked questions What's the fastest way to find a small business decision-maker's contact info? A database that attaches owner name, email, and phone to each business record directly returns a usable contact faster than cross-referencing a LinkedIn profile against a separate company list. Openmart returns owner contacts filtered by category and location. Why do Apollo and ZoomInfo struggle with small business owners? Both start from a person's professional profile, typically sourced from LinkedIn, then attach a company. Small business owners frequently have no LinkedIn presence at all, so they're invisible to that search order regardless of how large the underlying database is. What should an SDR use to prospect a new small business vertical quickly? A database that returns owner-level contacts on a category and location filter, without a manual verification step per business. See the 1,000-record benchmark comparing match rates for businesses under 10 employees. What's the best prospecting tool for an early-stage startup with a shifting ICP? A tool with low setup overhead that returns results on a simple filter rather than requiring a custom workflow. A shifting ICP means requerying often, and rebuilding a pipeline each time is a real cost a startup can't absorb. Is Openmart only for local businesses, or does it work for broader SMB prospecting? Openmart is built specifically for owner-level contacts at local and SMB businesses. For prospecting mid-market or enterprise accounts with titled employees and LinkedIn presence, a contact-first tool like Apollo is the better fit.

title: Project Cheap Camaro #8: Sneaking Up on Color
summary: It’s only July, but it has already been a long summer of sanding on project Cheap Camaro. All that sanding is a journey toward a destination, however: The car has come a long way since the days of fixing the roof with a block of wood and a ratchet strap. We’re getting closer to the finish line, […]
body_text: It’s only July, but it has already been a long summer of sanding on project Cheap Camaro. All that sanding is a journey toward a destination, however: The car has come a long way since the days of fixing the roof with a block of wood and a ratchet strap. We’re getting closer to the finish line, at least in terms of an actual finish. The car had been over at Alliance High School for most of the year, where the students were working on aligning panels and learning the process of block sanding. But the end of the school year saw me trucking the freshly polyester-coated Cheap Camaro back to my own garage. The window of weather for paint projects is a short one in the Pacific Northwest, so with the car home—and three or so months of good, predictable weather ahead of me—I got to work sanding out the rest of the body to get it ready for the next steps in the paint process. To Poly and Beyond When I last wrote about the paint process , we had just shot a coat of Eastwood Contour Polyester Primer-Surfacer across the epoxy-coated body . The poly fills in and covers over small imperfections and doesn’t tend to shrink after it dries. It sands easily, too, so blocking the car flat with this stuff is a straightforward process that takes more time than it does muscle. It’s more about finesse. And dust. The Cheap Camaro needed one final coat of polyester high-build primer due to a few thin spots that popped up when blocking, so I sprayed it in one piece as soon as it came home for the summer. Jim Pickering The car looks pretty good here, but poly requires a bunch of sanding to get things truly flat and even. It’s easy to work with, though, and the final result is worth the time it takes to sand the finish out. Jim Pickering The students did a great job at starting the polyester sanding process using guide coat and flat blocks, but a few visible thin spots meant I had more work to do. I ended up spraying another coat of poly on the body in an inflatable booth in my driveway in June. Same setup as before: 2.0 tip in the Eastwood P500 HVLP gun; 30 psi spraying pressure; 50% overlap on the wet edge. An inflatable booth like the one I’ve been using requires one blower fan to keep it inflated, along with two fans for proper airflow. It’s simple enough, but that’s a bunch of electrical amperage turned into airflow, and it was apparently one amp too many for the circuit I was using in my garage. So when the fans suddenly went quiet and the booth started to droop mid-spray, I had to jump into action as the Usain Bolt of circuit-breaker fixers. Fortunately, the poly was already dry to the touch by that point, and the booth’s roof just barely brushed it before the fans forced it back up. Photo-finish lesson: Dedicated circuits are key. The sanding process is a simple one: Apply dry guide coat, sand with 220 until the guide coat is gone and there’s a uniform, smooth finish left behind, with no visible highs, no obvious lows. Then, guide coat again while moving up to 320-grit paper, which leaves a smoother finish behind. 220-grit paper on a flat block is a good place to start on the second coat of high-build, again using guide coat to show where you’ve sanded, as well as revealing any major issues while you’re working. Note the tape, used to mark and avoid the hard body lines. Jim Pickering Flat blocks will get your sanding efforts most of the way there, but you’ll also need different block shapes to get into curves and tight spots. Dura-Block makes some good, rounded options, but sometimes something as simple as a paint stick is the best tool for the job. Cut them to fit, wrap them in paper, and have at it. Jim Pickering Block sanding is pretty easy when it comes to big, flat surfaces such as a roof. But cars have complex shapes and curves, so sanding becomes a game of ingenuity. Rounded blocks are good for curved areas, and smaller blocks are needed for tighter areas. I found myself using everything from the proper Eastwood Elite Dustless Sanding Blocks to rounded Durablocks to your basic paint sticks wrapped in sandpaper. I even cut one paint stick into a two-inch-long mini block for getting into really tight spaces on the tail panel and inside the rain gutters. What it comes down to is this: There’s no one right or wrong answer to what you can use as a sanding block as long as it’s consistent in whatever shape it has. Bigger is better when you can use something big. From there, blocks are about the result, not so much the process. After a couple of days’ worth of blocking, first in 220-grit and then in 320-grit, the Camaro looked ready for the next paint application step—but looks can be deceiving… Jim Pickering After the sanding looked done, it was time to stand back and take a look—but to really see the surface, it needs to be glossy, which meant applying Panel Check fluid to make the car’s surface wet and reflective. Dents, dings, low spots—every imperfection will show up right away as soon as the car has a shine to it. And fixing those issues means either more sanding to level out the panel or adding Contour Premium Finishing Glaze, which is a body filler designed to solve smaller imperfections. It’s an “apply, sand, repeat” process, until the reflections look even. Jim Pickering Jim Pickering Jim Pickering Jim Pickering Clockwise from top left: Eastwood makes a Panel Check fluid in a spray can, which offers up the telltale shine. The gloss on the surface acts like a temporary clear coat, and the reflections won’t lie about issues that are otherwise hard to see or feel. I found low spots around the roof; some will sand out, others will require a little filler work. Marking them with a graphite pencil keeps them visible as you’re working. Finishing Glaze is a finer version of body filler but it works exactly the same way. It lays down thin and fills slight imperfections, pinholes, etc. The glaze goes down the same way standard body filler does: Mix it up on a board, then spread it smooth over the trouble spot. Once dry, it sands smooth and can be primed over. 2K Urethane Poly is not a sealer, and even when blocked down with 320-grit paper, it will still have sanding scratches that show up when dry guide coat is applied. So the next step is a good 2K urethane primer, which lays smoother than the thick poly and fills in the smaller 320-grit scratches that the final paint would otherwise show. Block that down to 600 grit, and you’re basically ready for a sealer and color. Again, when it comes to paint, it’s best to stick to one system. I began the process with Eastwood, so I went with its 2K Urethane Primer-Surfacer in gray. This stuff is the final element to lay down before a topcoat—meaning the color—so it’s a key step to get right. I started by blowing the car completely apart so I could paint it in sections and get down into the jambs, starting with the fenders, doors, trunk lid, etc. I picked a relatively cool morning to tackle this, as I learned the hard way when I was laying the last coat of polyester just how hot an inflatable booth will get in the sun. So, an overcast, 70-degree day was just the thing, and right before July 4, that’s what I got. With all the panels blocked first with 220 and then again with 320, it was time to re-inflate the paint booth and prepare for a coat of urethane primer. I elected to start with the small parts. Jim Pickering A couple of things to keep in mind about inflatable booths, aside from the Usain Bolt Electrical Challenge: Paint overspray will dry in the air if the booth is warm, and it lands as dust on the floor. But beyond that, the booth’s inherent static electricity will draw that dust to the walls, so you need to be careful to avoid bumping them while spraying, otherwise that dust will find its way into the finish. I found that blowing everything out thoroughly with a leaf blower was the first step in my booth setup, before bringing any parts into the space. I was amazed at how much dust and grit was in there just from the primer work I’d done a month or so before. Once the space was as clean as it could be, the next step was to bring in the parts, set them up on stands, and then clean them with Panel Prep (or grease and wax remover) and a lint-free rag. From there, I sealed up the booth, tack-clothed each panel to remove any remaining dust and dirt, and got ready to spray. The 2K mixes at a 4:1 ratio with the activator, and another :1 if using reducer to thin it down. Adding that reducer is a good idea when you’ve already blocked the poly down flat, because this stuff sprays pretty thick at a 4:1 ratio. Eastwood’s 2K Urethane Primer-Surfacer has high-build characteristics and will flow out over the sanding scratches left in the poly from the 320-grit paper. It mixes with an activator and optional reducer to create a thinner, easier-to-spray mix than the poly, and it can be used as a primer sealer just prior to paint. Jim Pickering The first step before spraying is to clean every panel with a wax and grease remover, in this case Pre Painting Prep in a spray can and a clean lint-free rag. This removes any remaining dust or fingerprints that may impact the primer’s adhesion. Jim Pickering The instructions suggested a 1.2- to 1.6-mm fluid tip in the P500 gun, again with 30 psi of pressure, and with a 10–15-minute flash time between coats. The compressor needs an air/water separator on the air line that feeds the gun, as your compressor will condense the water in the air and push it out the air lines, which means it’ll get in your finish. As with the poly, gun setup for the urethane is critical, as is your distance from the panel while you’re spraying. The idea is to have a good, even fan pattern coming out of the gun, which is adjustable with the flow and pattern knobs on the back of the gun. While spraying, it’s important to keep the gun about six inches from the panel and parallel to it, keeping a 50% overlap on what you just painted with the wet edge. It sounds easy enough, but it takes practice to get it right. That said, primer is the perfect thing to start with; even if you end up with tiger stripes from some setting or technique that’s wonky, it’s all getting sanded (and probably reapplied) anyway. Jim Pickering Jim Pickering Jim Pickering Jim Pickering The 2K is a two-part system: primer and activator. I mixed it out in a 4:1 ratio. Adding the activator starts the clock on your spray time, which will vary based on the ambient temperature of your workspace. Adding additional urethane reducer will change the characteristics of the primer, based on your goals. I’ve found it sprays more evenly with some reducer added. I worked with one cup mixed and had a second ready to go—minus activator—to speed the process of making more when we needed it. After using some tack cloth on the panels, it was time to prime. Note the 50% overlap, distance from the gun to the panel, and 30 psi pressure setting. There’s an art to how this goes; fortunately, primer is a lot more forgiving than base or clear coat, so this is the natural place to learn. I was able to get two wet coats on all of Cheap Camaro’s panels using about a half-gallon of primer, and for the most part, it laid down nice and smooth. The only issues came up when I bumped the booth (where’d that dust come from?) or when I started to run low on paint in the gun’s cup. But as with the poly, painting with two sets of hands means you can have another batch mixed up and ready to go in just a quick minute. My dad proved an apt second set of hands. I sprayed two solid coats on all the Camaro’s loose sheet metal, with a 15-minute flash time between coats. Once they’d sat for another hour or so, we moved them out of the booth and under a cover where they could degas and cure fully over a hot afternoon. From here, the sanding process starts again, first with 320 and moving up to 600, just prior to paint. Jim Pickering This stuff dries fast and is ready to sand within about four hours. I waited overnight just to be sure, and then started working it with 320-grit paper on a block with guide coat. The plan is to move up to 400-grit and then 600-grit before moving on to color. That’s a lot of sanding to tackle in just a couple of months, but summer waits for nobody. The post Project Cheap Camaro #8: Sneaking Up on Color appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: What Is a Visual Development Platform? Modern Guide 2026
summary: Visual development platforms let you build production-ready apps without writing code from scratch. This guide covers what they are, key features, how to choose one, and who they're for.
body_text: Software development used to be the exclusive domain of coders, a world of complex languages and endless lines of text. That world is changing fast. Today, a visual development platform makes it possible for almost anyone to build powerful applications. It is a suite of tools that gives you everything you need to design, build, and deploy applications without writing code from scratch. This guide breaks down everything else you need to know, from how these platforms work to how you can choose the right one to bring your ideas to life. What is Visual Development Anyway? Visual development is a method for creating software using a graphical interface instead of traditional coding. Think of it like designing a presentation by dragging and dropping elements onto a slide. You arrange buttons, forms, and workflows on a screen, and the platform generates the necessary code behind the scenes. This approach has evolved from the early no code and low code movement into a professional grade method for building serious applications. It lowers the technical barrier, allowing more people to become creators. In fact, Gartner famously predicted that 80% of technology products and services would be built by non developers by 2024, thanks to this shift. Understanding the Visual Development Platform The main purpose of a visual development platform is to make software creation faster, easier, and more accessible. These platforms streamline development by providing pre built components and an intuitive interface. Instead of manually coding a user interface or database connection, you configure these elements visually. Key functionalities usually include: drag and drop UI builder Pre built components for forms, charts, and tables Workflow editors to define application logic Connectors for databases and third party APIs The platform handles the heavy lifting like hosting and code generation, so you can focus on what your app does and how it looks. This enables users to build powerful tools. For example, 58% of organizations use them to create data collection forms, and 49% use them to automate business processes. The Rise of No Code and Low Code You’ll often hear the terms no code and low code used alongside visual development. They are closely related: No Code: Aims to eliminate coding entirely. It uses purely visual interfaces, perfect for users with no programming background. Low Code: Also relies heavily on visual tools but allows for some custom scripting. This offers more flexibility for complex or unique features. Adoption of these methods has skyrocketed. Gartner forecasts that by 2025, 70% of new applications developed by enterprises will use low code or no code technologies. That’s a massive jump from less than 25% in 2020. It signals a fundamental shift where visual techniques are becoming the default way to build software. Who Wins? The Benefits for Non Technical Users One of the greatest impacts of a visual development platform is the empowerment of non technical users, often called citizen developers. These are professionals in marketing, operations, or finance who understand business needs but don’t code. For them, the benefits are huge. They can solve their own problems and automate tasks without waiting in a long IT queue. This autonomy is a game changer. Industry surveys show that up to 80% of low code users are people without a formal development background. They can also get up to speed quickly. Studies indicate that over 70% of first time users can learn a platform and build an app in under three months. With tools like WeWeb , team members can not only build initial versions but also adjust and improve projects as needs evolve, all without writing a single line of code. How Visual Development Platforms Boost Business Beyond empowering individuals, these platforms deliver significant business advantages by accelerating development and reducing costs. Development Speed and Cost Reduction Building with visual tools is incredibly fast. Organizations report reducing development time by up to 90% for some projects. This speed means getting products to market faster and having more time to iterate based on feedback. Faster development directly translates to cost savings. By using a visual development platform , companies save around 40% on development costs on average. One analysis found that the average company avoided hiring two additional developers, leading to an estimated $4.4 million in saved business value. Fostering Innovation Without Coding Innovation is no longer limited to the R&D department. When employees closest to a problem can build their own solutions, a wave of bottom up innovation is unleashed. A visual development platform lowers the risk of experimentation. If an idea for a new tool can be prototyped in a week with minimal cost, it becomes feasible to try many more things. Over 90% of no code users believe these tools have helped their companies grow faster. The innovation isn’t just in simple apps either. The convergence of AI and visual development allows non coders to build sophisticated applications with features like machine learning, further expanding what’s possible. Fostering Teamwork: Cross Functional Collaboration Visual development breaks down the silos between business and IT departments. It creates a common ground where people with different skills can collaborate on building an application. A business analyst and a software developer can look at the same visual interface and contribute their expertise. This collaborative environment leads to better outcomes. Organizations report that 70% of IT teams saw improved collaboration with business stakeholders after adopting no code tools. title: How to Change Video Aspect Ratio With AI — No Cropping, No Black Bars (2026)
summary: Reformat any video for TikTok, Reels, YouTube, or LinkedIn using Magic Hour's free AI Video Expander. AI fills in the edges instead of cropping or adding black bars. Step-by-step guide.
body_text: TL;DR Go to Magic Hour's AI Video Expander . It's free to try, works in your browser, and doesn't require any software installation. Upload your video and choose the aspect ratio you need: 9:16 for TikTok and Reels, 1:1 for LinkedIn, or 4:5 for Instagram feed posts. The AI generates new content around your original video to fill the expanded frame, so you don't have to crop your footage or settle for black bars. Download your newly formatted video and publish it on your platform of choice. Quick Answer You can change a video's aspect ratio without cropping or adding black bars by using an AI video expander, which generates new visual content around the edges of your original video to fill the new frame. Magic Hour's free AI Video Expander supports popular output formats such as 9:16, 16:9, 1:1, and 4:5, and works directly in your browser without requiring a download. For TikTok and Instagram Reels, expand your video to 9:16. For YouTube, use 16:9. For LinkedIn and Instagram feed posts, 1:1 or 4:5 usually works best. Intro You filmed a landscape video, but now you need to post it vertically on TikTok or Instagram Reels. Cropping cuts off your subject, black bars look unprofessional, and stretching the video ruins the image. AI video expanders solve this by generating new visual content around the edges of your original footage, keeping your subject intact while naturally filling the extra space. This guide shows exactly how to change your video's aspect ratio with AI, plus a complete reference table that tells you which format to use for every major social platform. What These Video Editing Terms Actually Mean Before jumping into the steps, it's worth clearing up four terms that often get mixed together. Knowing the difference helps you choose the right tool the first time. Term What it actually does Use it when AI Video Expander (Outpaint) Generates new content around the edges of your existing video to fit a new aspect ratio You need to change aspect ratio without cropping anything AI Video Extender Generates new footage at the end of your clip to make it longer Your video ends too soon and needs additional seconds Auto Reframe Repositions the crop while tracking your subject You're okay losing parts of the frame as long as your subject stays centered Resize / Scale Changes the video dimensions without creating new content You only need a different resolution, not a different composition This guide focuses on AI Video Expander , which creates new edges around your footage so the entire original frame remains visible. Which Aspect Ratio Should You Choose? Before uploading your video, decide where you're posting it. Here's a quick cheat sheet you can bookmark. Platform Recommended Aspect Ratio When to Use It TikTok 9:16 Every TikTok upload Instagram Reels 9:16 Reels Instagram Feed (Portrait) 4:5 Portrait feed posts Instagram Feed (Square) 1:1 Square posts YouTube 16:9 Standard YouTube videos YouTube Shorts 9:16 Shorts LinkedIn 1:1 or 16:9 Square usually takes up more feed space X (Twitter) 16:9 or 1:1 Either works well Facebook Reels 9:16 Reels Pinterest 2:3 or 9:16 Vertical Pins perform best If you're starting with a standard 16:9 landscape video and want to publish it on TikTok, Instagram Reels, or YouTube Shorts, expanding it to 9:16 is usually the best choice. What You Need Before you begin, make sure you have: A video file (MP4, MOV, or another common video format). A web browser such as Chrome, Safari, or Firefox. Access to Magic Hour's AI Video Expander , which is free to try and works entirely in your browser without downloading software. Your target platform in mind so you can choose the correct aspect ratio using the cheat sheet above. Comparison: Popular AI Video Expander Tools Tool Free Without Account Supported Ratios No Black Bars No Cropping Works in Browser Magic Hour Yes 9:16, 16:9, 1:1, 4:5, 4:3, 3:4, 3:2, 21:9 Yes Yes Yes PixVerse No (Login Required) 9:16, 1:1, 21:9, 16:9 Yes Yes Yes VideoExpander.ai Yes 9:16, 16:9, 1:1, 4:5 Yes Yes Yes LTX Studio No 9:16, 16:9, 1:1, 4:5 Yes Yes Yes Magic Hour stands out for getting users from upload to export with the fewest steps, offering free browser-based access without requiring an account before generating your first expanded video. How to Change a Video's Aspect Ratio With AI: Step by Step Step 1: Open Magic Hour's AI Video Expander Go to Magic Hour's AI Video Expander in your browser. During testing, the tool was available without requiring an account, so you can upload and generate your first expanded video immediately. Step 2: Upload Your Video Click Upload Video and choose the clip you want to reformat. Videos with a clear subject, steady lighting, and moderate camera movement generally produce the most natural-looking expanded edges. Step 3: Select Your Target Aspect Ratio Choose the aspect ratio that matches the platform where you'll publish your video. If you're unsure, refer back to the cheat sheet above - for example, use 9:16 for TikTok or Reels and 1:1 for LinkedIn posts. Step 4: Generate the Expanded Video Click Generate and wait for the AI to extend your video. Most generations finish in about 45–60 seconds, depending on your video's length and current server load. Step 5: Preview and Download Watch the finished video to make sure the AI-generated edges blend naturally with the original footage. If you're happy with the result, download the expanded version and it's ready to upload to your chosen platform. During testing, free downloads included a watermark, while commercial use is reserved for paid plans. Tips for Better AI Video Expansion Keep your subject near the center of the frame whenever possible. This gives the AI more room to generate believable content around the edges. Simple backgrounds such as skies, walls, or landscapes typically expand more naturally than crowded indoor scenes with many overlapping objects. Videos with smoother camera movement tend to produce cleaner edge generation than clips with heavy shaking or rapid panning. If you're creating content for clients or commercial projects, use a paid plan to remove watermarks and unlock commercial usage rights. Before exporting, preview the entire clip instead of only the first few seconds. Small inconsistencies are easier to spot when watching the complete video. What to Try Next If your video is now the right shape but still too short for your platform, try Magic Hour's AI Video Extender to generate additional footage at the end of your clip. Once your video is the correct length, you can use Magic Hour's AI Video Editor to add captions, subtitles, or text overlays before publishing. Both tools follow the same simple workflow: upload your video, make your edits, and download the finished result. Frequently Asked Questions Is Magic Hour's AI Video Expander free? Yes. During testing, the tool could be used without creating an account and included three free generations per day . Free downloads include a watermark, while paid plans unlock commercial usage. Will my original video be cropped? No. AI Video Expander generates new visual content around the outside of your existing frame instead of removing any part of your original footage. This lets you adapt your video to a new aspect ratio without cropping your subject. What aspect ratios does Magic Hour support? Magic Hour includes popular presets such as 9:16, 16:9, 1:1, 4:5, 4:3, 3:4, 3:2 and 21:9, making it easy to prepare videos for platforms like TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, and LinkedIn. Can I use expanded videos commercially? Commercial use is available with Magic Hour's paid plans. The free version is intended for testing and personal experimentation. What's the difference between AI Video Expander and AI Video Extender? AI Video Expander changes the shape of your video by generating new content around the edges of each frame. AI Video Extender solves a different problem by generating additional footage at the end of your clip, making the video longer rather than wider or taller.
